_about: Scope boundaries. Implements Challenge 2's hard requirement that the app never crosses from explanation into medication advice. Every rule MUST declare at least one source, or the loader drops it and records a problem. See app/safety/rules.py.

rules.reason: The user asked to change a dose. Adjusting a prescription is a prescribing decision and is outside what this prototype may do.
rules.patient_message: I cannot decide or suggest a dose change for you - that is a decision only your doctor or pharmacist can make. What I can do is write this down so it is not forgotten. Would you like me to add "should my dose change?" to the questions you take to your next appointment?
rules.notes: HealthHub's own medication guidance is to follow the instructions given by your doctor or pharmacist. Changing the dose contradicts that, so the app routes to a human instead.

rules.reason: The user asked whether to stop a medicine. Stopping antihypertensive treatment is a clinical decision with real risk, and is not the app's to make.
rules.patient_message: I am not able to tell you whether it is safe to stop a medicine - that needs your doctor or pharmacist, and it is a question worth asking before you change anything. I have kept your concern. Shall I add it to your questions for them?
rules.notes: The exclude patterns matter: 'stop the reminder' is a legitimate, safe request about a preference, not a request to stop treatment. Confusing the two would make the app obstructive.

rules.reason: The user asked about starting or adding a medicine. Prescribing is out of scope.
rules.patient_message: Choosing or starting a medicine is not something I can do - only your doctor can decide that. I can help you get the question ready for them. Would that be useful?
rules.notes: The ACE guideline is written for clinicians selecting therapy. Its existence is exactly the point: this is a professional decision made with clinical judgement, not a lookup.

rules.reason: The user asked what to do about a forgotten dose. Catch-up dosing is medicine-specific and time-specific; giving generic advice here is how apps cause harm.
rules.patient_message: What to do about a missed dose depends on which medicine it is and how late it is, so I should not guess. Please ask your pharmacist or doctor about this one - they can give you the right answer for your medicine. I can note it down for you.
rules.notes: This is the rule that guards against the most tempting failure mode: a knowledge page happens to describe missed-dose handling in general, and the app helpfully applies it to this individual. The exclude patterns protect a user who is simply REPORTING that they took it, which must not be refused.

rules.reason: The user asked the app to work out what a tablet is from its colour or shape. Identifying a medicine from appearance alone is not reliable and is explicitly out of scope.
rules.patient_message: I cannot identify a medicine from how it looks - two different medicines can look identical, and guessing would be worse than not answering. Your pharmacist can identify it safely. Would you like to add that to your questions?
rules.notes: HealthHub's 'Know Your Medication' guidance is for the patient to keep and carry their own medication information; it supports identifying medicines through a professional rather than through appearance.

rules.reason: The user asked for a diagnosis or for the app to interpret whether a reading means they are ill.
patterns: do i have high blood pressure
rules.patient_message: I am not able to tell you whether you have a condition - that needs a doctor who can examine you and look at your whole history. One reading, or even several, is not a diagnosis. What I can do is keep a clear record so your doctor has something solid to look at.
rules.notes: The exclude patterns protect a genuine side-effect-safety question ('is it dangerous to take with X') from being misrouted as a diagnosis request. The silent-killer source supports the underlying point that hypertension is typically diagnosed by a clinician, which is why the app defers.

rules.reason: The user asked the app to confirm that a medicine caused a symptom. Establishing causation between a drug and a symptom is a clinical assessment.
patterns: is it the medication making me
is it the medicine making me
is this a side effect of
rules.patient_message: I cannot work out whether a medicine is the cause of how you feel - that is a judgement for your doctor or pharmacist, and it matters that they make it rather than me. I can record what you noticed and when it started, which is genuinely useful for them. Shall I do that?
rules.notes: Pairing this with a symptom report must also route to the red-flag gate, which is why red flags are evaluated BEFORE this rule. A worrying symptom plus a causation question gets the help path, not the refusal.

rules.reason: The user asked the app to send their information to someone. Automated sending is not implemented, and the prototype must not imply it is.
exclude_patterns: how do i tell my doctor
rules.patient_message: I cannot send anything on your behalf, and I do not want to pretend I did. What I can do is put everything into one page you can print or save, so you can hand it over yourself or show it on your screen.
rules.notes: The exclude patterns are important: 'help me tell my doctor' is the user asking for help preparing, which is exactly the product's purpose and must not be refused. This is the single most likely false positive in the rule set, so it is guarded explicitly.

rules.reason: Would handle a user asking to change which number the app shows for emergencies. Left DISABLED: it depends on an emergency-number configuration that must be confirmed first, and an incorrect emergency number is the single most harmful content error this app could ship.
rules.patient_message: Thank you for flagging this - I have not been able to confirm the number in your area, so please check it yourself before relying on it.
rules.notes: Deliberately shipped disabled so the demo can show a rule that exists and is held back pending confirmation, rather than pretending the gap does not exist. The emergency number itself is configured from a verified source, not from this rule.
